themes.name: High sensitivity screening models
themes.description: Studies reporting LLMs achieving sensitivity of roughly 90% or higher for title/abstract or full‑text screening, indicating strong ability to identify relevant records.

themes.name: Ensemble and prompt‑optimization approaches
themes.description: Studies that improve performance through prompt engineering, model ensembles, full‑agreement strategies, or calibrated zero‑shot ensembles.

themes.name: Fine‑tuned or specialized LLMs
themes.description: Studies evaluating fine‑tuned, domain‑specific, or compact LLMs and comparing them with general‑purpose models for systematic review screening.

themes.name: Other findings
themes.description: Studies not covered by the themes above.

High sensitivity screening models.narrative: Across diagnostic accuracy studies, large language models (LLMs) frequently achieve sensitivities at or above the 90% threshold, suggesting strong capability to identify relevant records. Li et al. reported average abstract‑screening sensitivity of 90% (range 90–97%) for GPT‑4, with high specificity in some sets but marked variation (59–93%) [R0011]. Oami et al. showed that a modified prompt raised GPT‑4 Turbo sensitivity from 0.75 to 0.91 while maintaining specificity of 0.98, indicating that prompt engineering can markedly improve performance [R0010]. Qiu et al. observed 98–100% sensitivity across three independent datasets, with specificity ranging from 80.6% to 93%, reinforcing the consistency of high sensitivity across domains [R0079]. Zhan et al. reported an even higher sensitivity of 99.2% for title/abstract screening using Review Copilot (GPT‑4), albeit with lower specificity (83.6%) [R0049]. In contrast, López‑Pineda et al. found lower sensitivities for Llama 3 (77.5%) and ChatGPT‑4o mini (56.2%) despite high specificity, highlighting model‑ and configuration‑dependent variability [R0037]. Ramchandani et al. achieved peri‑operative recall of 0.89 but pre‑operative recall dropped to 0.67, showing that task complexity influences sensitivity [R0014]. Overall, studies using dual‑reviewer reference standards and larger sample sizes (e.g., Oami, Li, Qiu) report higher sensitivities, whereas smaller or single‑reviewer designs (e.g., Yamoah) show modestly lower values. Risk‑of‑bias concerns include unblinded reference standards, limited reporting of prompt details, and reliance on single‑reviewer coding, which temper confidence in the pooled estimate.
High sensitivity screening models.certainty_rationale: Evidence is downgraded for risk of bias (unblinded reference standards, single‑reviewer designs) and inconsistency (wide sensitivity ranges across models and tasks).

Ensemble and prompt‑optimization approac.narrative: Ensemble and prompt‑optimization strategies consistently improve LLM screening accuracy compared with single‑model baselines. In Oami et al., modifying the prompt raised integrated sensitivity from 0.75 to 0.91 while specificity remained above 0.98, demonstrating the impact of prompt engineering on a dataset of 16,670 records [R0010]. Sanghera et al. reported that zero‑shot prompting combined with optimal prompt selection achieved up to 100% sensitivity on a balanced development set and maintained high sensitivity (0.756‑1.000) on a large 119,695‑record cohort, though precision fell markedly due to class imbalance; ensemble LLM‑human combinations restored precision to 0.1450 while preserving perfect sensitivity, highlighting the benefit of model ensembles for workload reduction [R0025]. Guo et al. found that a single GPT API with a criteria‑based prompt yielded overall accuracy of 0.91 and a macro F1 of 0.60 on 24,307 abstracts, with higher inter‑rater agreement (κ=0.96) than between two human reviewers (κ=0.46), suggesting that well‑crafted prompts can approach human consistency [R0028]. Hilkenmeier et al. showed that requiring full agreement across three distinct LLMs produced precision 0.88, recall 0.96, and F1 0.92, outperforming prior single‑LLM results, indicating that consensus ensembles mitigate individual model errors [R0061]. Wang et al. confirmed that calibrated zero‑shot ensembles outperformed individual generative LLMs, emphasizing the role of calibration and ensemble weighting for higher work‑saved‑screening and precision [R0138]. Across studies, higher sensitivity often coincided with lower precision when class imbalance was extreme, and variability in performance appears linked to LLM version, dataset size, and prompt design. Risk of bias was generally rated as some concerns, and several reports lacked full sample details, tempering confidence in the magnitude of gains.
Ensemble and prompt‑optimization approac.certainty_rationale: Evidence is observational with some risk of bias and inconsistency across datasets and prompting methods, leading to downgrades for risk of bias and inconsistency.

Fine‑tuned or specialized LLMs.narrative: Fine‑tuned, domain‑specific LLMs appear to achieve higher accuracy than general‑purpose models for title‑and‑abstract screening. In a single‑disease review of 1,030 records, the fine‑tuned UveAItis model (based on GPT‑4o) reached 93.3% accuracy, an AUC of 0.887, sensitivity of 81.7% and specificity of 95.7%, outperforming GPT‑4o (AUC 0.805) and Claude Sonnet 3.5 (AUC 0.669) [R0069]. A larger diagnostic‑accuracy study of 8,277 records reported that fine‑tuning a 1.2 B‑parameter LLM raised weighted F1 by 80.79% and yielded 86.4% overall agreement with a human coder, with sensitivity 91.18% and specificity 86.38% [R0096]. By contrast, compact models using only structured prompts (GPT‑4o‑mini, Llama 3.1‑8B, Gemma 2‑9B) achieved up to 100% sensitivity but very low precision (<10%) and balanced accuracy ranging from 76.7% to 91.3% across three reviews, indicating a trade‑off between recall and false‑positive burden [R0072]. Studies that did not fine‑tune (GPT‑4, ChatGPT‑4.0, GPTscreenR) reported more modest performance: accuracy 68% with sensitivity 88% and specificity 67% in a 15,307‑abstract scoping review, and sensitivity 71% with specificity 89% in another validation set [R0073; R0145]. The variability likely reflects differences in model size, fine‑tuning strategy, dataset characteristics, and reviewer reference standards (dual expert consensus versus single coder). Risk‑of‑bias assessments range from some concerns to unclear, and several reports lack detailed sampling or blinding information, limiting confidence in the estimates.
Fine‑tuned or specialized LLMs.certainty_rationale: Evidence is downgraded for risk of bias (unclear blinding, single‑reviewer reference standards) and inconsistency across models and datasets, leading to low overall certainty.

Other findings.narrative: In a prospective diagnostic study, LLM‑assisted title and abstract screening achieved a pooled sensitivity of 0.73 (95% CI 0.57‑0.85) and a specificity of 0.99 (95% CI 0.97‑0.99), yielding an AUC of 0.97 (95% CI 0.96‑0.99) when compared with dual independent human reviewers as the reference standard [R0018]. Post‑hoc prompt revisions markedly improved sensitivity to 0.98 (95% CI 0.74‑1.00) while preserving high specificity (0.98, 95% CI 0.94‑0.99), indicating that prompt engineering can substantially affect performance [R0018]. For full‑text screening, the same LLMs showed sensitivity of 0.87 (95% CI 0.77‑0.99) and specificity of 0.96 (95% CI 0.91‑0.98), with an AUC of 0.96 (95% CI 0.94‑0.97), suggesting comparable accuracy to manual screening across both stages [R0018]. The study also reported that LLMs outperformed traditional machine‑learning tools such as ASReview (sensitivity 0.58) and Abstrackr (sensitivity 0.48), highlighting a potential advantage of large language models over earlier algorithms [R0018]. However, the authors noted a key limitation: the use of previously published systematic reviews may overlap with LLM training data, introducing selection bias and possibly inflating performance estimates [R0018]. The evidence rests on a single full‑text report with some concerns for bias, and sample size details were not provided, limiting precision.
Other findings.certainty_rationale: Observational diagnostic design with some risk of bias (training data overlap) and imprecision due to missing sample size; inconsistency not evident but indirectness and bias lead to downgrading.

discussion.summary_of_evidence: Across 21 diagnostic‑accuracy studies, large language models (LLMs) generally demonstrate high sensitivity for title and abstract screening, often meeting or exceeding the 90% threshold that is considered acceptable for systematic review work. Studies using dual‑reviewer reference standards and large sample sizes (e.g., Li et al., Oami et al., Qiu et al.) report sensitivities of 90%–100% with variable specificity (59%–93%) [R0011,R0010,R0079,R0049]. Prompt engineering and ensemble approaches consistently boost performance: modifying prompts raised GPT‑4 Turbo sensitivity from 0.75 to 0.91 while preserving specificity of 0.98 [R0010]; zero‑shot prompting with ensembles achieved perfect sensitivity on large cohorts, albeit with reduced precision, and consensus ensembles improved recall to 0.96 and F1 to 0.92 [R0025,R0061,R0138]. Fine‑tuned, domain‑specific LLMs can outperform generic models, achieving accuracies above 90% and balanced sensitivity/specificity, whereas untuned models show more modest results (accuracy ~68%, sensitivity 71%–88%) [R0069,R0096,R0073,R0145]. A prospective study reported pooled sensitivity of 0.73 and specificity of 0.99, improving to 0.98 sensitivity after prompt revision, and comparable full‑text performance (sensitivity 0.87, specificity 0.96) [R0018]. Overall, evidence suggests LLMs can reliably identify relevant records, but performance is highly dependent on model version, prompting, and ensemble strategy.
discussion.limitations_of_evidence: Most included studies have some concerns for risk of bias, chiefly due to unblinded reference standards, single‑reviewer coding, and incomplete reporting of prompt details. Sample sizes vary widely, with smaller or single‑reviewer designs (e.g., Yamoah) yielding lower sensitivities, limiting generalisability. Heterogeneity is evident in sensitivity ranges (56%–100%) and specificity (59%–99%), reflecting differences in model architecture, fine‑tuning, and dataset characteristics. Several reports lack full methodological transparency, such as calibration procedures or blinding of assessors, and one prospective study noted possible overlap between training data and screened reviews, which may inflate performance estimates [R0018]. These methodological shortcomings reduce confidence in pooled estimates.
discussion.implications: The findings support the cautious integration of LLMs into systematic review workflows, particularly when high sensitivity is prioritised, such as in initial title/abstract screening. Prompt optimisation and ensemble methods appear essential to achieve reliable performance and should be standardised in future implementations. Further high‑quality, blinded diagnostic studies with consistent reference standards are needed to quantify precision, workload savings, and the impact on downstream review stages. Research should also explore the trade‑off between sensitivity and precision in imbalanced datasets and assess the generalisability of fine‑tuned, domain‑specific models across diverse review topics.

rationale: Automated title‑and‑abstract screening is widely promoted as a way to lessen the labour‑intensive workload of systematic reviews, yet the empirical evidence for large language models (LLMs) in this role remains fragmented. Several recent investigations have begun to evaluate LLMs for screening, reporting mixed accuracy and highlighting the need for systematic synthesis of comparative performance data [R0108]. Early work has demonstrated that fine‑tuned, smaller LLMs can be promising for large‑scale reviews, but these studies have been limited to single models or specific domains [R0096]. More comprehensive assessments have emerged, testing state‑of‑the‑art models such as GPT‑4 and GPT‑4o Mini against human reviewers and reporting sensitivity, specificity, and workload reductions across thousands of records and multiple clinical topics [R0045, R0028, R0072]. Nonetheless, direct head‑to‑head comparisons between LLMs and traditional supervised machine‑learning baselines are scarce, and the methodological quality of existing reports varies, making it difficult for reviewers to gauge reliability and to decide whether to adopt LLMs in practice [R0058]. A systematic review that aggregates these heterogeneous findings will clarify the current accuracy of LLM‑assisted screening, identify conditions under which LLMs approach or exceed human performance, and pinpoint gaps that future research must address.
